items.prompt: What does fault injection do?
choices: Forces a dependency to fail in a controlled test
Speeds up the whole suite by skipping every slow network call
Counts how many lines the tests ran
items.explanation: It stages a failure on purpose and checks how the caller reacts.

items.prompt: Which is the right question for a fault-injection test?
choices: How many lines of the service did the full suite run?
Is the dependency fast enough?
What does the caller do when the dependency fails?
items.explanation: It probes the caller's behavior under failure.

items.prompt: The waiter never stops waiting for a silent kitchen. What was missing?
choices: A friendlier and shorter dinner menu
A rule for when to stop waiting
More waiters on shift
items.explanation: Nothing bounded the wait, so silence froze every waiter.

items.prompt: Why can 100% line coverage miss an outage?
choices: It does not say which failure situations were staged
It only counts the slowest lines in the whole suite of tests
It ignores lines with network calls
items.explanation: Coverage records that lines ran, not what the dependency did.

items.prompt: Which kind of test double does fault injection use?
choices: One that always returns a successful answer
One that records nothing at all
One that returns a failure on purpose
items.explanation: The same seam is used, pointed at failure.

items.prompt: When is fault injection run?
choices: Only on the live system after release
In a controlled test, before release
Only when a customer complains
items.explanation: It catches known failure risks before they ship.

items.prompt: A suite tests only successful dependency answers. How well is failure handling tested?
choices: Not at all
Fully, since the code ran
Partly, through validation errors
items.explanation: Success-only tests never exercise the failure branches.

items.prompt: Why stage the failure on purpose?
choices: Failures never happen in a production system
Tests cannot call dependencies
The real one is rare and uncontrolled
items.explanation: A deliberate fault gives a repeatable, safe way to see the reaction.

items.prompt: A service has 100% line coverage. Its pricing call has no time limit. What can you say about a pricing outage?
choices: The tests cover it, since the call line ran during them
The suite never created one, so the reaction is unknown
The service is safe, because coverage reached every line
The reaction is known to be graceful from the coverage report
items.explanation: Coverage shows the line ran in a success scenario. Nobody staged the dependency going silent, so nothing about that reaction was ever checked.
items.reference:
Coverage versus staged scenarios
coverage: which lines ran during tests
fault injection: which failures were staged on purpose
a hung call still 'runs' its line, so coverage looks full
Why: a fully covered service can still never have seen its dependency fail.
items.learnMore:
What fault injection adds

Line coverage records that the network-call line ran. Fault injection stages the situation in which that call never answers, an error comes back, or the body is unusable, and checks the caller's reaction.

Common mistake

Reading a high coverage number as proof that failures are handled. Coverage says nothing about which situations were created.
items.reflection: Think of a drill or rehearsal you have seen. Which breakdown did it never practice, and what would it take to stage it safely?

items.prompt: Team A reuses a stub that always answers correctly. Team B swaps in a stub that never answers. What does B check that A cannot?
choices: Whether the caller handles correct data with a clean shape
Whether the stub class is built the way the framework needs
Whether the caller survives a dependency that goes silent
Whether the suite can run without the real dependency up
items.explanation: Both use the same seam. Only the second asks what the caller does under failure.

items.prompt: A bug report says: all connections stuck while the vendor was down. Which earlier practice would have caught it?
choices: Raising the line coverage number from 95% to 100%
Adding more tests for valid and invalid customer input
Retrying the vendor call in the existing success test
Staging a vendor that never answers and watching the caller
items.explanation: The stuck connections come from an unbounded wait. Only a staged silence exposes it; coverage and input tests do not.

items.prompt: A manager says the suite covers errors because it tests rejection of a bad card number. What is wrong with that claim?
choices: Rejecting bad input is not a dependency failing
Bad cards are too rare to count as a real error case
The card check is slower than a dependency failure test
It proves the code returns errors but not that it logs them
items.explanation: Validation errors come from the code's own rules. Fault injection is about a dependency misbehaving, which is a different path.

items.prompt: Which failure mode is 'accepts the call, never answers'?
choices: Hang
Error response
Malformed body
items.explanation: A hang is silence with no end.

items.prompt: Which failure mode returns a failure status?
choices: Hang
Connection refused
Error response
items.explanation: The dependency answers, but with a failure.

items.prompt: Which failure mode means the dependency is down or unreachable?
choices: Slow late response
Connection refused
Malformed body data
items.explanation: The call fails before any answer exists.

items.prompt: Which failure mode answers 'success' with unusable data?
choices: Malformed body
Hang
Error response
items.explanation: The status looks fine but the content is broken.

items.prompt: Which failure mode answers correctly but long after a sensible wait?
choices: Connection refused
Error response
Slow response
items.explanation: It answers, just very late.

items.prompt: How many distinct failure modes does the unit list?
choices: Three
Five
Seven
items.explanation: Hang, error response, refused connection, slow response, malformed body.

items.prompt: What does a hang test check that an error-status test does not?
choices: Whether there is a time limit
Whether the status code is read at all
Whether the body is parsed
items.explanation: A hang exercises the waiting, not the status.

items.prompt: Does one injected fault stand in for the others?
choices: Yes, they all share one path
Yes, if it is the hang
No, each runs different code
items.explanation: Each mode is its own bug waiting to happen.

items.prompt: A caller checks the status of every response and throws on failure. Which fault still gets through?
choices: A dependency that answers with a failure status
A dependency that never answers
A dependency that replies 500 on every call
A dependency that returns an authorization error
items.explanation: The status check needs a response to look at. A hang produces none, so the call just keeps waiting.
items.reference:
Five ways a dependency fails
hang: never answers
error response: answers with a failure status
connection refused: unreachable
slow response: answers far too late
malformed body: 'success' with unusable data
Why: each mode runs different code in the caller, so one handled mode proves nothing about the others.
items.learnMore:
One mode does not cover another

Checking a response status runs only after a response arrives. A hang never gets there, a refused connection fails before any status exists, and a malformed 200 passes the status check with bad data inside.

Common mistake

Believing that handling error statuses means the caller is safe against everything a dependency can do.
items.reflection: Think of a person or service you rely on. In how many different ways can it let you down, and which have you planned for?

items.prompt: A dependency returns 200 OK with a body missing the price field. The caller's status check passes. Which failure mode is this?
choices: Error response
Hang
Malformed body
Slow response
items.explanation: The status says success while the content is unusable, so only a check on the data's shape would catch it.

items.prompt: A caller wraps its call in a try block that handles a refused connection and an error status. Which test would still show a gap?
choices: A dependency that refuses the connection outright
A dependency that returns a 503 status code
A dependency that is shut down before the call
A dependency that answers after 90 seconds
items.explanation: Refusal and failure statuses are both handled. A very late answer is neither, and needs its own decision about when slow counts as failed.

items.prompt: A team wrote one injection test, for a 500 status, and counts the failure handling as done. What is the most accurate assessment?
choices: One mode of five is tested; the other four stay unknown
All five are tested, since a 500 is the most general fault
Failure handling is tested except the retry behavior
Two of five are tested, because 500 implies a refusal too
items.explanation: Each mode runs different defensive code, so a 500 test says nothing about hangs, refusals, slowness or bad bodies.

items.prompt: Which is a graceful reaction to a failing dependency?
choices: Wait with no limit at all
Crash the process
Return a cached value
items.explanation: A fallback keeps the failure contained.

items.prompt: Which is a broken reaction?
choices: Return a clear error
Wait with no limit
Fall back to a default
items.explanation: An unbounded wait is a hang.

items.prompt: What does a cascade mean?
choices: One failure drags down unrelated requests
A retry that succeeds after one short delay
A cached answer returned
items.explanation: The failure spreads instead of staying contained.

items.prompt: What is silent corruption?
choices: Returning a clear and typed error
Retrying with delays
Reporting success with wrong data
items.explanation: The failure hides behind a success.

items.prompt: What makes a retry graceful?
choices: Back-to-back attempts with no spacing at all
Spaced attempts that eventually stop
Attempts that never end
items.explanation: Spacing gives the dependency room to recover.

items.prompt: What does fail fast do?
choices: Stops calling for a while after repeated failures
Retries forever until the dependency finally answers
Hides the error
items.explanation: It protects both sides from useless calls.

items.prompt: Is a clear error to the caller graceful?
choices: No, any visible error counts as broken
Only if it crashes
Yes, it is visible and bounded
items.explanation: A clear failure is contained and honest.

items.prompt: What do graceful reactions share?
choices: They never show any error to the caller
The failure stays contained
They always succeed
items.explanation: They are visible, bounded in time and not spreading.

items.prompt: A service retries 5 times with no gap, then gives up. A test only asserts that it gave up. What does that test miss?
choices: Whether the service eventually stopped trying
Whether the service returned some kind of error
Whether the attempts were spaced out
Whether the dependency was actually called at all
items.explanation: A tight loop stops too, so 'it gave up' passes it. Spacing is the property that separates helping from adding load.
items.reference:
Contained or spreading?
graceful: retry with spacing, fallback, fail fast, clear error
broken: hang, crash, silent corruption, cascade
5 tight retries: 0 ms spacing; 5 backed-off: 1,500 ms total spacing
Why: graceful failures stay visible, bounded and contained; broken ones spread or hide.
items.learnMore:
Testing the reaction

A fault test names the expected reaction in advance and checks that exact behavior, including its shape. For a retry, that means both that it stops and that attempts are spaced.

Common mistake

Calling a reaction graceful because it eventually stopped. A tight retry loop stops too and still hammers a struggling dependency.
items.reflection: Think of a time something at work or home went wrong. Did the failure stay contained, or did it spread, and what decided that?

items.prompt: Doubling gaps of 100, 200, 400 and 800 ms separate 5 attempts. How long does the caller wait in the gaps in total?
choices: 800 ms
items.explanation: 100 + 200 + 400 + 800 = 1,500 ms between five attempts.

choices: Silent corruption, since it reports success with wrong data
Fallback, since it answered quickly with something
Fail fast, since it avoided calling the dependency
Clear failure, since the caller got a response
items.explanation: A fallback or error is honest about the degraded state. An empty list shown as a success hides the failure and misleads the caller.

items.prompt: Which observation best shows a cascade?
choices: The failing endpoint returns a clear error quickly
Unrelated endpoints time out while one dependency is failing
The failing endpoint returns a cached value
The failing call is retried three times then dropped
items.explanation: A cascade is the failure spreading beyond the call that failed, taking down work that never touched the dependency.

items.prompt: Is a fault-injection test flaky?
choices: Yes, because it goes red when it fails on purpose
Yes, it uses timing
No, its failure is deliberate and controlled
items.explanation: Flaky means accidental and uncontrolled.

items.prompt: What is a seam?
choices: A type of timeout in a network client
A swap point for a dependency
A kind of network error
items.explanation: It lets a test replace the real dependency.

items.prompt: What does a normal double return?
choices: A successful answer
A hang
A crash
items.explanation: Its job is isolation and speed.

items.prompt: What does a fault double return?
choices: Only the correct answers it was given
Nothing it was told to
A hang, error or bad body
items.explanation: Its job is to break on purpose.

items.prompt: Which runs on a live system?
choices: Fault injection tests
Chaos engineering
Flaky tests
items.explanation: Chaos breaks real systems to find unknowns.

items.prompt: What does a flaky test do to trust?
choices: Weakens it
Builds it
Leaves it unchanged
items.explanation: A red run might mean nothing.

items.prompt: Can code with no seam be fault-injected?
choices: Yes, with no change to the code at all
Yes, using coverage
Not until a seam exists
items.explanation: There is nothing to swap.

items.prompt: Fault injection catches which kind of risk?
choices: Unknown risks after release
Known risks before release
Only slow tests
items.explanation: Chaos engineering covers unknown risks.

items.prompt: A test goes red on every run because the stub hangs on purpose, and the code has no time limit. How should it be described?
choices: Flaky: it fails and the cause is timing
Correct: it reliably exposes a real gap
Broken: a test must never go red on purpose
Chaos: it breaks a live system to see what happens
items.explanation: A deliberate, controlled fault that reliably fails on a genuine bug is working as designed. Flaky tests fail without anyone intending it.
items.reference:
Four neighbours, four intents
flaky test: accident, uncontrolled, destroys trust
normal double: answers well, keeps tests fast
fault injection: on purpose, controlled, pre-release
chaos engineering: on purpose, live system, finds unknowns
Why: the same seam serves different questions; intent and control separate the ideas.
items.learnMore:
Seam first

Swapping a dependency needs a swap point. Without a seam, the network call is welded into the code and neither a stub nor a fault double can stand behind it.

Common mistake

Treating a test that fails on a hang as flaky. If it fails reliably on a deliberate fault, it is doing its job.
items.reflection: Think of a tool you use both to practice normally and to rehearse a breakdown. What did you have to change to turn one into the other?

items.prompt: A team wants fault injection but the code calls the network inline, with no way to replace the call. What comes first?
choices: Run the tests more times to see what fails
Raise the line coverage for that module
Create a seam so the dependency can be swapped
Switch to chaos engineering on the live system
items.explanation: Injection works by substituting what stands behind the swap point. With no swap point, a seam must be introduced first.

The language the stand-ins are written in
How many lines of the caller they cover
The question each asks of the caller
items.explanation: The substitution mechanism is identical. The first isolates the caller; the second checks its failure handling.

items.prompt: Why does the hang test have its own guard?
choices: To make the passing tests run a lot faster
To count retries
So a failing test cannot freeze the suite
items.explanation: Without it, a hung function hangs the test run.

items.prompt: What does the fix add to the naive function?
choices: A second pricing service
A time limit and a fallback
More logging and nothing else
items.explanation: Bounded wait plus a sensible reaction.

items.prompt: What happens at the timeout when a price was remembered?
choices: It returns the last known price, flagged stale
It waits again forever for the pricing service reply
It crashes checkout
items.explanation: The stale flag lets the caller tell.

items.prompt: What happens at the timeout when nothing was remembered?
choices: A guessed price based on the product name
A silent success
A clear 'pricing unavailable' error
items.explanation: A clear failure is the last resort.

items.prompt: Which proves the fix works?
choices: A brand new unrelated test also passes today
The same test passes after failing before
Line coverage rises
items.explanation: Same test, before and after.

items.prompt: Does the naive function handle an error status?
choices: Yes, it throws on one
No, it ignores statuses
Only on retries
items.explanation: Its flaw is the missing time limit.

items.prompt: What problem does a too-short timeout cause?
choices: Hung calls stay open far longer than they need to
The fallback never runs
Slow but working calls are treated as failed
items.explanation: Users see stale prices unnecessarily.

items.prompt: What problem does a too-long timeout cause?
choices: Slow but working calls fail much too early
Hung calls hold connections for longer
The cache stops working
items.explanation: It is the L1 pile-up, only capped.

items.prompt: The function now has a 500 ms limit. The test guard is still 300 ms. What does the re-run report?
choices: It passes, since the guard is shorter than the limit
It fails because the function's limit is too long
It reports a stale price, as the fallback ran
The guard fires first and blames the function for a hang it would have handled
items.explanation: A guard shorter than the function's limit ends the test before the fix can act, so the guard must be set longer, such as 700 ms.
items.reference:
Guard, limit and fallback
test guard: fires first on a failing run so the suite never freezes
function limit: 500 ms in the worked fix
test guard must outlast it: 700 ms, not 300 ms
fallback: last known price, flagged stale; error if none
Why: two separate limits do two jobs, and the guard must be longer than the limit it is verifying.
items.learnMore:
The fix and its edges

A bounded wait plus a fallback turns the hang into a visible, limited event. The test then proves the fix by passing where it failed before. The reaction to choose (stale price, retry, clear error) is a product call.

Common mistake

Setting the test guard shorter than the function's limit, so the test fires first and blames a function that was about to handle the failure.
items.reflection: Think of a safety net you have set up for something risky. What would happen if the net were shorter than the thing it was catching?

items.prompt: On the payment step, the pricing service times out and a stale price exists. What is the best judgment?
choices: Prefer a clear 'try again' if the real price may have moved
Always charge the stale price, since staying up wins
Always crash checkout, since a stale price is a bug
Always guess a fresh price from the last two values
items.explanation: A stale price on a listing is a fair trade for staying up. Charging on one at payment can be worse than asking the user to retry. The test only checks the chosen behavior happens.

items.prompt: With the demo's assumed numbers (250 ms typical slow end, 8% of calls spiking to 1,200 ms), which timeout avoids all unnecessary fallbacks?

1,200 ms or more
500 ms
Any value above 100 ms
items.explanation: In that model a 500 ms timeout still falls back unnecessarily for about 5.9% of calls; only at 1,200 ms or above are none wasted, at the cost of holding hung connections longer.

items.reference:
Guard, limit and fallback
test guard: fires first on a failing run so the suite never freezes
function limit: 500 ms in the worked fix
test guard must outlast it: 700 ms, not 300 ms
fallback: last known price, flagged stale; error if none
Why: two separate limits do two jobs, and the guard must be longer than the limit it is verifying.
items.learnMore:
The fix and its edges

A bounded wait plus a fallback turns the hang into a visible, limited event. The test then proves the fix by passing where it failed before. The reaction to choose (stale price, retry, clear error) is a product call.

Common mistake

Setting the test guard shorter than the function's limit, so the test fires first and blames a function that was about to handle the failure.
